newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech crown up on GDP data, mkt refocuses on trade.
newsitem.headline: Czech crown up on GDP data, mkt refocuses on trade.

text.p: The Czech crown strengthened on Friday after better than expected 1996 growth figures calmed fears on the foreign exchange markets of an imminent cut in interest rates.

Immediately after the statistical bureau reported that gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 4.4 percent last year, compared with market expectations of less than three percent, the crown firmed by around 75 basis points against its mark/dollar basket, putting it at 29.5 against the dollar and 17.4 against the mark.
"I think the (GDP) figures are of course better than expected..it was a surprise for the market," said Tomas Becvar of Komercni Banka.

Czech GDP growth slowed sharply over the first three quarters of last year, prompting widespread calls for the Czech National Bank (CNB) to relax monetary policy, which was tightened in the middle of 1996.
Dealers said Friday's figures, showing growth rising to 4.7 percent in the fourth quarter from 3.6 in the third, had dampened speculation of a cut in rates.
"It looks like the Czech economy is performing not that poorly...so it makes less space for cutting interest rates," said Breta Tichanek of ING Bank.
In June last year, the discount rate was raised to 10.5 percent from 9.5 and in August minimum reserve requirements were increased by three percentage points to 11.5 percent.
The moves have succeeded in fulfilling the CNB's primary policy aim of reining in money supply and bringing inflation lower.

M2 money growth slowed to 7.8 percent in December from 20.2 percent in the same month of 1995 and inflation fell to 7.3 percent year-on-year in February from more than nine percent at the beginning of 1996.

However, the tightening of monetary policy has created a wide interest rate differential with the Czech Republic's main trading partners, keeping the crown high and making life difficult for exporters.
The Czech trade deficit soared to just over 160 billion crowns ($5.4 billion) in 1996 and in January it nearly doubled from the same month in the previous year to 13.6 billion crowns.
Tichanek said the crown was likely to hold its early gains for the rest of Friday but he expected little further movement until the release of foreign trade figures for February on Monday morning.
The Czech crown is fixed daily against the mid-point of a basket comprising 65 percent marks and 35 percent dollars. It can be fixed 7.5 percent either side of the basket mid-point.
Earlier this year the crown hit a high of 5.51 percent above the basket mid-point but has subsequently weakened because of fears over the trade deficit and official interest rate policy.
On Friday, the crown was fixed at 29.4 to the dollar and 17.41 to the mark, putting it 0.88 percent above the basket mid-point.
